stops.name: London: landfall in exile
stops.campa: Freud reaches London on 6 June, met at Victoria Station by a small, relieved crowd of English colleagues, and takes temporary rooms at 39 Elsworthy Road in Hampstead while a permanent house is found. He is eighty-two, in constant pain from the cancer, and has lost his home of forty-seven years, his language of daily life, and most of his sisters' safety in a single season, yet he writes almost at once that the relief of feeling, for the first time since March, that no knock at the door can mean the Gestapo, outweighs everything else that has been lost.
stops.quote: The feeling of triumph on being liberated is too strongly mixed with grief.

stops.name: London, 20 Maresfield Gardens: the couch reassembled
stops.campa: The family moves into a tall red-brick house in Hampstead, 20 Maresfield Gardens, and Freud's study is rebuilt almost exactly as Berggasse 19 had stood: the same crowded shelves of Egyptian, Greek, and Roman antiquities, the same rug-covered analytic couch, the same desk facing the garden. He resumes seeing a handful of patients within weeks of arrival, working now against the clock of his illness on Moses and Monotheism, the strange last book in which the founder of psychoanalysis argues that Moses himself was an Egyptian, and that monotheism's God is the murdered father returning, endlessly, in the guilt of the sons.

stops.name: London, Maresfield Gardens: the end
stops.campa: By September the cancer, declared inoperable months before, has eaten through the cheek into a wound that will not heal, the pain no longer bearable and no longer, Freud says, making any sense. He tells his physician Max Schur he wishes to be released, asks him to consult Anna, and Schur, keeping a promise made years earlier never to let him suffer needlessly, administers morphine on the night of the 21st and again on the 22nd. Freud dies in the small hours of 23 September 1939, eleven days after Hitler's armies cross into Poland, the century he diagnosed already at war around him.
stops.quote: Now it is nothing but torture and makes no sense any more.
stops.quote_source: Freud to Max Schur, September 1939, recounted in Schur, Freud: Living and Dying (1972)
